name: Daria Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. This is confidential. Tell me about a normal day at Park Court.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I put the kettle on when I get in and start with yesterday's bank entries. I'm Daria Usman, forty-three, and I prepare tax returns and accounts for small landlords at Park Court Accounts. I did a bachelor's in accounting years ago, then worked in factory payroll until a layoff brought me here. I'm a junior on lower pay now; payroll and tax look alike on paper, but I still need my supervisor on the odd repairs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a ledger that balances after a careful question. I don't like guessing why a landlord has coded a boiler repair as a new asset. I have never used the AI tool on the office screen; I prefer the routine I know. Omar is a plumber, our children are nine and thirteen, and our mortgage leaves less than one month of bills saved. There are few accounting firms close enough to try if this one cuts hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small change is easier for me to picture. The firm has a sorting tool, but I still use the ledger and ask my supervisor when I cannot place a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it is sensible to keep a person checking a tax return before it reaches a client. I'd tell the partners that modest savings should make the filing week less frantic, if the tool really helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI is not the thing that keeps me awake in this picture. I'm forty-three, junior at Park Court Accounts and still learning tax returns after years doing payroll inside a factory. My pay is low, we have less than a month's bills saved, and there are few similar firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the handwritten ledger checks and ask my supervisor to review rental-property files with odd repairs. This month I'd stop the paid television package and hold the thirty in our mortgage account. In the first year of a plateau, I'd keep doing the ordinary tax work and ask for a steadier filing schedule around the children's school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the house, though my work might continue. Omar's plumbing wage is steadier than mine, but it cannot pay the mortgage and school costs alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What drained the last savings you had?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pipe in our own kitchen leaked last spring, and the replacement parts took the tiny savings we had. Omar could fix the labour himself, but he still had to buy the parts. The mortgage did not wait for the tap to stop dripping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the television cut change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the television provider to stop the package at the end of this billing month. Thirty is small, but it is money we can actually see. I would not tell the children the house is in trouble over one cancelled channel.

I would seek a steadier **filing schedule** for school pickup.
think: Our **mortgage** is a worry even without major AI change.
Few **nearby firms** make my low-paid junior post important.
do: Keep **handwritten ledger checks** and supervisor review.
Cancel the **television package** and hold thirty for mortgage.
Ask for a **steadier filing schedule** around school pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the house despite steady work.
S0.quote: The mortgage did not wait for the tap to stop dripping.
fieldNote: A **kitchen leak** used the household’s last savings despite her partner doing the labour.
She avoids **AI tools** and relies on ledger checks while learning the new tax role.

steps.text: Keep handwritten ledger checks and supervisor review on tax files
Cancel television package and hold thirty monthly for mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the machine writes, checks and answers, it sounds like most of the jobs on my side of the room. I am not the quickest junior even without a new screen to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to show us which duties will go before changing hours. To friends I'd say people need time and wages to learn another job, not a cheerful lesson at the end of a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours could be cut while the senior accountants keep the client meetings. I have a bachelor's in accounting, but factory payroll was a different kind of work, and I am still getting used to tax cases. A cut of one day a week would leave our mortgage short, even with Omar working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor to list the tax mistakes I need to fix this month. I'd take the list to the staff meeting and ask the partners for paid training before any hours are cut. If they still cut a day, I'd apply for the funded payroll vacancy at the packaging plant, but only if the wage covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I cannot tell my children I am calm when one fewer workday means a payment problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your child notice at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child, Yasmin, notices when I skip the grocery shop's fresh fruit shelf. I'd explain that we are keeping the house paid and not blame her for asking. I wouldn't give her a number I cannot promise to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What conditions matter for the other job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the mistake list to be written down so I can practice the right things. If the packaging plant post is only temporary or pays less than the mortgage needs, I will not leave a current wage for it. I would stay and ask the firm for the paid training hours.

say: I would request a **duty list** before the partners change junior hours or move work to software.
I would seek **paid training** before junior cuts.
think: Losing **one workday** could leave our mortgage short.
My **factory payroll** experience has not made me quick at tax cases.
do: Study **written tax mistakes** with my supervisor if paid practice hours are approved.
Ask at the **staff meeting** for paid training before cuts.
Apply for **stable funded plant payroll** work after a day’s cut only if wage covers mortgage.
feel: I feel **anxious** that a possible one-day cut would leave the mortgage short.

fieldNote: Her **prior payroll experience** does not erase junior tax mistakes or exposure to automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 is too soon for this firm to work out a fair process. If AI can do almost all thinking work, it could prepare the returns before I have learned to check them properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say employers should give clear notice and the government should help people keep their homes during a sudden job change. At work I'd ask for dates and a named person to answer staff questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior tax post to end in the first year after full AGI in 2028. The work is at a desk, so robots arriving around 2031 do not extend it. Omar's plumbing work may last longer, but one wage will not cover our mortgage, food and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the children's paid weekend swimming lessons after this term and hold the fifty monthly for the mortgage. I'd apply now for the open medical-supply inventory post if it is funded and its pay covers our payment, though its ordering screen may change too. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I'd claim wage support and ask the lender for temporary terms before we miss an instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and embarrassed to say it. I have a short list of calls, but nothing on it guarantees a wage before the next payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your partner take extra shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar would offer to work Saturdays, but his shoulder has been sore and those shifts are not guaranteed. I'd tell him I don't want the mortgage carried by an injury. We would tell the children about swimming after we had the next month's budget written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the inventory post usable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The inventory post needs a published wage and start date. If it is only a three-month contract, I would keep my present job while looking for another opening. I will not leave my current wage for a three-month inventory contract.

say: I would request **clear notice** and housing help before families miss a mortgage payment.
I would ask for **dates and contacts** at work.
think: My **junior desk job** could end soon after 2028, before I have learned the tax role fully.
One **plumber’s wage** cannot cover all household costs.
do: Pause **swimming lessons** after term and hold fifty monthly.
Seek **funded inventory work** with published mortgage-covering wage and start date; keep current job if contract lasts only three months.
Claim **wage support** and ask lender for temporary terms after dismissal.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing the mortgage wage.
S2.quote: I will not leave my current wage for a three-month inventory contract.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches her tax desk in 2028; later robots do not extend that job.
The **plumbing fallback** has limits because extra shifts are uncertain and her partner’s shoulder hurts.

steps.text: Pause swimming lessons after term and hold fifty monthly for mortgage
Apply for funded inventory post with published mortgage-covering wage and start date
Seek wage support and lender terms after 2028 dismissal before missed payment
Keep current job and search other openings if inventory contract lasts only three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives the firm time to tell us what is changing. I still expect the routine returns I do to go when full AGI arrives in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say employers should pay for a genuine transition and name the vacancies it leads to. I would ask for a written training plan, not a list of links to read at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could return to payroll in a larger workplace before 2031, though payroll itself is thinking work and may shrink too. I would rather move to a funded post than chase a new qualification without a job. The robots in 2034 do not give my tax desk extra time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in the current payroll rules course if Park Court pays the three-hundred fee and gives paid study hours. I'd ask my old factory contact for one supervised payroll close if the employer permits it. In the first year after AGI in 2031, if my tax role ends, I'd apply for a funded payroll vacancy only if its wage covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less rushed. I know payroll, and a few years might let me prove I can still do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you cover the course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three hundred would come straight from the money for the next bill. I would ask the partners for the fee and paid hours on one form. If they refuse, I would keep my current role and use free payroll guidance before applying anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the payroll visit prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supervised close would show whether the rules changed while I was away. I'd want a written reference from the payroll manager, not just a friendly coffee. That would help me judge whether a real employer would take me back.

I would demand a **written training plan**.
think: A **payroll post** could be a temporary bridge even though payroll screens also face AGI.
My **bill money** cannot fund course fees upfront.

Seek a **supervised payroll close** with employer permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets us think in school years instead of filing seasons. The children would be older, but the mortgage would still be there unless we changed how we pay it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for clear notice and affordable training places long before 2036. I'd say a firm that saves on account preparation should help people leave with a real job, not just a final cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my tax desk to shrink when thinking AI arrives in 2036. I might be able to move back into factory payroll sooner, though that screen work is exposed too. Robots around 2039 do not protect either desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my current ledger routine this year and ask the packaging plant next spring about a funded payroll traineeship with paid hours. I'd join only if the wage covers our mortgage and the supervisor can give me real files to learn on. In the first year after 2036, if my tax post ends, I'd take a funded payroll vacancy if one remains; otherwise I'd claim wage support and keep searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a decade gives me room to ask careful questions. I am not going to announce a new career before there is a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yasmin and our younger son would be adults or nearly so, but I would not plan on their wages. I want them to see us keep the house paid without handing them our bills. A longer runway should serve the children, not turn them into a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide a traineeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what the traineeship pays during training and what wage follows. If the employer cannot name a funded vacancy, I would stay where I am and try again later. A familiar job is only useful if it still has a payslip.

I would ask firms for a **real job path** after cuts.
think: My **tax desk** still faces AGI in 2036.
A **payroll return** needs a funded wage, not familiarity alone.
do: Keep the **ledger routine** and current job if no funded traineeship job path exists.

S4.quote: A familiar job is only useful if it still has a payslip.
fieldNote: A **ten-year horizon** supports a cautious return to payroll, subject to funded work and supervised files.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My desk work would go before I found a solid replacement, and Omar's wage cannot cover the mortgage alone. Notice, wage support and a funded vacancy with paid training would help. I would rather have a clear wage offer than a promise that some new work will appear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how much uncertainty a family can carry. We have already used the savings once on a kitchen leak. I can learn a new workplace in time, but we cannot move the mortgage date to suit a hopeful prediction.

headlineQuote: I would rather have a clear wage offer than a promise that some new work will appear.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Daria is a junior accountant at Park Court after a factory payroll layoff.
Her **accounting bachelor’s** and payroll history have not yet made her quick at tax returns.
She earns **low pay**, never uses AI and prefers handwritten ledger checks.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and less than one month saved keep ordinary risks close.
Few **nearby firms** make her favor funded wages and cautious moves back toward payroll.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her junior desk role before a stable replacement appears.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **notice**, wage support and a funded vacancy with paid training.
